category: Mapping, Robotics & Navigation Toolboxes > Geospatial, Kinematics & Autonomy
description: Geographic plotting, raster and vector map data and coordinate reference systems; rotation and transformation representations; robot kinematics and motion planning; occupancy maps; and inertial sensor fusion filters.

tools.name: geoplot
tools.description: Plot lines and markers on a geographic axes using latitude and longitude coordinates, over an interactive basemap. Panning and zooming automatically reload basemap tiles at the appropriate resolution. It is the simplest way to draw tracks, routes and boundaries on a map.
tools.usage:
geoplot(lat, lon)
geoplot(lat, lon, LineSpec)
geoplot(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2, ...)
geoplot(___, Name, Value)
geoplot(gx, ___)

parameters.name: lat, lon
parameters.description: Latitude and longitude vectors in degrees.

parameters.name: LineSpec
parameters.description: Line style, marker and colour, e.g. 'r-o'.

tools.name: geoscatter
tools.description: Create a scatter plot on a geographic axes, with marker size and colour driven by data values. It is the geographic equivalent of a bubble chart and is ideal for showing magnitude at point locations such as earthquakes, stations or sales. Combine with a colorbar to give the colour scale meaning.
tools.usage:
geoscatter(lat, lon)
geoscatter(lat, lon, sz)
geoscatter(lat, lon, sz, c)
geoscatter(___, Name, Value)

parameters.name: sz
parameters.description: Marker area in points squared, scalar or per point.

parameters.name: c
parameters.description: Colour: a name, RGB triplet, or a data vector mapped through the colormap.

parameters.name: 'MarkerFaceAlpha'
parameters.description: Marker transparency, useful when points overlap.

tools.name: geobasemap
tools.description: Select the background map displayed behind geographic plots. Several basemaps such as 'darkwater' and 'bluegreen' are stored locally, while 'streets', 'satellite' and 'topographic' are streamed from an online service. Choose the basemap that gives enough context without competing with your data.
tools.usage:
geobasemap(basemapName)
geobasemap(gx, basemapName)
bm = geobasemap(gx)
tools.example:
gx = geoaxes;
geoplot(gx, [51.5074 48.8566], [-0.1278 2.3522], 'y-', 'LineWidth', 3)
geobasemap(gx, 'satellite')
% Local basemaps that need no internet connection:
geobasemap(gx, 'colorterrain')
tools.notes: The streamed basemaps require an internet connection; use the locally stored ones in offline environments.

tools.name: geoaxes
tools.description: Create a geographic axes object with latitude and longitude rulers, a basemap and an appropriate map projection. It gives programmatic access to properties such as limits, basemap, grid and label formatting. Use it when you need to configure a map more precisely than the plotting functions allow.
tools.usage:
gx = geoaxes
gx = geoaxes(Name, Value)
gx = geoaxes(parent, ___)
geoaxes(gx)

tools.name: geolimits
tools.description: Set or query the latitude and longitude limits of a geographic axes, which controls the visible map extent and the basemap zoom level. Called with no arguments it returns the current limits. Use it to frame a region precisely rather than relying on autoscaling.
tools.usage:
geolimits(latlim, lonlim)
geolimits(gx, latlim, lonlim)
[latlim, lonlim] = geolimits
geolimits('auto')

tools.name: readgeoraster
tools.description: Read a geospatial raster file such as GeoTIFF, DTED, USGS DEM or ESRI grid, returning the data array together with a spatial referencing object. The referencing object ties array indices to geographic or projected coordinates. Use it for elevation models, satellite imagery and gridded climate data.
tools.usage:
[A, R] = readgeoraster(filename)
[A, R] = readgeoraster(filename, Name, Value)
info = georasterinfo(filename)

parameters.name: 'Bands'
parameters.description: Which bands to read from a multiband file.

tools.name: shaperead
tools.description: Read vector geographic data from an ESRI shapefile into a geographic or map data structure array, with one element per feature. Each element carries the geometry plus all the attribute fields from the associated database file. Selector and bounding-box options let you filter features while reading.
tools.usage:
S = shaperead(filename)
S = shaperead(filename, Name, Value)
S = shaperead(filename, 'UseGeoCoords', true)

parameters.name: 'UseGeoCoords'
parameters.description: Logical; true returns Lat/Lon fields instead of X/Y.

parameters.name: 'Attributes'
parameters.description: Cell array naming which attribute fields to keep.

tools.name: projcrs
tools.description: Create a projected coordinate reference system object from an EPSG code or WKT string, describing a planar map projection with its datum and units. Use it with projfwd and projinv to convert between geographic and projected coordinates. It is how you attach a well-defined CRS to projected data.
tools.usage:
p = projcrs(code)
p = projcrs(code, 'Authority', authority)
p = projcrs(wkt)
[x, y] = projfwd(p, lat, lon)
[lat, lon] = projinv(p, x, y)

parameters.name: code
parameters.description: EPSG code, e.g. 32619 for UTM zone 19N or 3857 for Web Mercator.

parameters.name: wkt
parameters.description: Well-known text description of the CRS.

tools.notes: geocrs creates geographic (unprojected) reference systems such as EPSG 4326.

tools.name: distance
tools.description: Compute the great-circle or rhumb-line distance between points on a sphere or ellipsoid, with an optional azimuth output. The result is in degrees of arc by default, or in physical units when a reference ellipsoid is supplied. It is the standard geodesic distance calculation in Mapping Toolbox.
tools.usage:
[arclen, az] = distance(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2)
[arclen, az] = distance(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2, ellipsoid)
[arclen, az] = distance(track, ___)
arclen = distance(___, units)

parameters.name: lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2
parameters.description: Start and end coordinates in degrees.

parameters.name: ellipsoid
parameters.description: A referenceEllipsoid such as wgs84Ellipsoid('km'), which makes the output a physical length.

tools.name: azimuth
tools.description: Compute the azimuth (bearing) from one point to another along a great circle or rhumb line, measured clockwise from north. Great-circle azimuth changes continuously along the path, while rhumb-line azimuth is constant. Use it for navigation headings and for orienting directional antennas.
tools.usage:
az = azimuth(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2)
az = azimuth(lat1, lon1, lat2, lon2, ellipsoid)
az = azimuth(track, ___)
az = azimuth(___, units)

tools.name: deg2km
tools.description: Convert an arc length in degrees to a distance in kilometres along the surface of a sphere of given radius. It is the usual companion to distance when you have left the result in degrees. km2deg performs the inverse conversion.
tools.usage:
km = deg2km(deg)
km = deg2km(deg, radius)
km = deg2km(deg, sphere)

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: Sphere radius in kilometres (default: Earth's radius).

tools.name: quaternion
tools.description: Create quaternion objects for representing 3-D rotations without gimbal lock and with efficient composition and interpolation. Quaternion arrays support multiplication, conjugation, normalization, rotation of vectors and spherical linear interpolation. They are the standard attitude representation in navigation and robotics.
tools.usage:
q = quaternion(a, b, c, d)
q = quaternion(matrix)
q = quaternion(RV, 'rotvec')
q = quaternion(angles, 'euler', seq, pointOrFrame)
q = quaternion(rotmat, 'rotmat', pointOrFrame)
v = rotatepoint(q, pt)

parameters.name: 'euler' / 'eulerd'
parameters.description: Build from Euler angles in radians or degrees.

tools.name: quat2rotm
tools.description: Convert quaternions to 3-by-3 rotation matrices, returning a 3-by-3-by-N array for N input quaternions. Rotation matrices are what most kinematics and transformation code consumes directly. The input quaternion must be normalized for the result to be a valid rotation.
tools.usage: rotm = quat2rotm(quat)

parameters.name: quat
parameters.description: N-by-4 matrix of quaternions in [w x y z] order, or a quaternion object.

tools.notes: Robotics System Toolbox uses [w x y z] ordering; be careful when interfacing with libraries that use [x y z w].

tools.name: rotm2eul
tools.description: Extract Euler angles from rotation matrices for a specified rotation sequence. The returned angles are in radians and follow the intrinsic rotation convention of the chosen sequence. Beware of gimbal lock, where the decomposition becomes ambiguous.
tools.usage:
eul = rotm2eul(rotm)
eul = rotm2eul(rotm, sequence)

tools.name: eul2quat
tools.description: Convert Euler angles to quaternions for a given rotation sequence, returning an N-by-4 matrix in [w x y z] order. Converting to quaternions avoids the gimbal-lock and interpolation problems of Euler angles. The companion functions eul2rotm and eul2tform produce rotation matrices and homogeneous transforms.
tools.usage:
quat = eul2quat(eul)
quat = eul2quat(eul, sequence)

parameters.name: eul
parameters.description: N-by-3 matrix of Euler angles in radians.

tools.name: se3
tools.description: Represent a 3-D rigid body transformation (rotation plus translation) as an SE(3) object that composes with the multiplication operator. It can be built from a homogeneous matrix, from a rotation and translation, or from Euler angles or quaternions. Methods such as transform, inv, interp and dist make transformation chains concise and readable.
tools.usage:
tf = se3
tf = se3(rotation, translation)
tf = se3(T)
tf = se3(eul, 'eul', trvec)
T = tform(tf)
pts = transform(tf, points)
tfInv = inv(tf)

parameters.name: rotation
parameters.description: A 3-by-3 rotation matrix, so3 object or quaternion.

tools.notes: Introduced in R2022b. Older code uses raw 4-by-4 matrices with trvec2tform, tform2trvec, rotm2tform and tform2rotm.

tools.name: tform2trvec
tools.description: Extract the translation vector from one or more homogeneous transformation matrices. Together with tform2rotm and tform2quat it decomposes a transform into its rotation and translation parts. trvec2tform performs the inverse construction.
tools.usage:
trvec = tform2trvec(tform)
rotm = tform2rotm(tform)
tform = trvec2tform(trvec)

tools.name: rigidBodyTree
tools.description: Represent a robot manipulator as a tree of rigid bodies connected by joints, supporting forward kinematics, Jacobians, dynamics and collision checking. Bodies are added with addBody and joints are configured with setFixedTransform. It is the central data structure of Robotics System Toolbox.
tools.usage:
robot = rigidBodyTree
robot = rigidBodyTree('DataFormat', fmt, 'MaxNumBodies', n)
addBody(robot, body, parentName)
T = getTransform(robot, config, bodyName)
J = geometricJacobian(robot, config, bodyName)
show(robot, config)
config = homeConfiguration(robot)

parameters.name: 'DataFormat'
parameters.description: 'struct' (default), 'row' or 'column'; row/column vectors are required for dynamics functions.

parameters.name: 'Gravity'
parameters.description: [x y z] gravity vector for dynamics computations.

parameters.name: body
parameters.description: A rigidBody object with a rigidBodyJoint attached.

tools.notes: loadrobot and importrobot provide ready-made models of common commercial robots and URDF import.

tools.name: inverseKinematics
tools.description: Solve for the joint configuration that places a specified robot body at a desired pose, using a damped least-squares or Levenberg-Marquardt solver. Per-axis weights let you prioritize position over orientation or ignore a redundant degree of freedom. It returns solution information reporting whether the target pose was actually reached.
tools.usage:
ik = inverseKinematics('RigidBodyTree', robot)
[configSol, solInfo] = ik(endEffectorName, pose, weights, initialGuess)
ik.SolverParameters

parameters.name: 'RigidBodyTree'
parameters.description: The robot model to solve for.

parameters.name: initialGuess
parameters.description: Starting configuration; a good guess is essential for convergence.

parameters.name: solInfo.Status
parameters.description: 'success' or 'best available' when the target could not be reached exactly.

tools.notes: generalizedInverseKinematics adds constraints such as aiming, joint bounds and Cartesian bounds.

tools.name: importrobot
tools.description: Import a robot model from a URDF, SDF or Simscape Multibody model file into a rigidBodyTree, including visual and collision meshes. This is how you bring in manipulator models exported from CAD or published by robot vendors. The optional mesh path argument resolves relative references to geometry files.
tools.usage:
robot = importrobot(filename)
robot = importrobot(filename, Name, Value)
[robot, importInfo] = importrobot(simscapeModel)

parameters.name: 'MeshPath'
parameters.description: Folder(s) in which to look for referenced mesh files.

tools.notes: loadrobot provides a curated library of commercial robots without needing external URDF files.

tools.name: occupancyMap
tools.description: Represent a 2-D environment as a probabilistic occupancy grid, where each cell stores the probability that it is occupied. Probabilities are updated from sensor observations using log-odds arithmetic, with configurable saturation limits. It is the standard map representation for SLAM and for sampling-based path planning.
tools.usage:
map = occupancyMap(width, height, resolution)
map = occupancyMap(p, resolution)
setOccupancy(map, xy, values)
val = getOccupancy(map, xy)
insertRay(map, pose, scan, maxRange)
show(map)
inflate(map, radius)

parameters.name: 'OccupiedThreshold' / 'FreeThreshold'
parameters.description: Probabilities above/below which a cell is considered occupied or free.

parameters.name: 'ProbabilitySaturation'
parameters.description: [min max] clamp on cell probabilities so the map stays adaptable.

parameters.name: 'GridLocationInWorld'
parameters.description: World coordinates of the map's bottom-left corner.

tools.notes: occupancyMap3D handles volumetric maps; binaryOccupancyMap is the lighter-weight binary alternative.

tools.name: binaryOccupancyMap
tools.description: Represent an environment as a binary occupancy grid where each cell is simply free or occupied. It uses much less memory than a probabilistic map and is what most path planners and the pure pursuit controller expect. Use inflate to grow obstacles by the robot's radius so the planner can treat the robot as a point.
tools.usage:
map = binaryOccupancyMap(width, height, resolution)
map = binaryOccupancyMap(p, resolution)
setOccupancy(map, xy, occ)
occ = getOccupancy(map, xy)
inflate(map, radius)
show(map)

parameters.name: width, height, resolution
parameters.description: Map size in world units and cells per unit.

parameters.name: p
parameters.description: A logical matrix defining the initial grid.

parameters.name: radius
parameters.description: Inflation radius in world units, typically the robot's radius.

tools.name: plannerRRTStar
tools.description: Plan a collision-free path with the asymptotically optimal RRT* algorithm, which rewires the search tree as it grows so the path converges toward the optimum. It requires a state space and a state validator describing the map and collision rules. Use it when path quality matters more than raw planning speed.
tools.usage:
planner = plannerRRTStar(stateSpace, stateValidator)
planner = plannerRRTStar(___, Name, Value)
[pathObj, solnInfo] = plan(planner, startState, goalState)

parameters.name: stateSpace
parameters.description: e.g. stateSpaceSE2 or stateSpaceDubins defining the configuration space.

parameters.name: stateValidator
parameters.description: e.g. validatorOccupancyMap, which checks states and motions against the map.

parameters.name: 'ContinueAfterGoalReached'
parameters.description: Logical; keep optimizing after the first solution is found.

tools.notes: plannerRRT is faster but non-optimal; plannerHybridAStar suits car-like vehicles with curvature limits.

tools.name: controllerPurePursuit
tools.description: Compute linear and angular velocity commands that steer a differential-drive robot along a series of waypoints, by aiming at a point a fixed lookahead distance along the path. The lookahead distance trades path-following accuracy against smoothness. It is the standard geometric path-following controller for mobile robots.
tools.usage:
controller = controllerPurePursuit
controller = controllerPurePursuit(Name, Value)
[v, omega] = controller(pose)
[v, omega, lookaheadPoint] = controller(pose)

parameters.name: 'Waypoints'
parameters.description: N-by-2 matrix of [x y] path waypoints.

parameters.name: 'LookaheadDistance'
parameters.description: Distance ahead on the path to aim at; larger gives smoother but less accurate tracking.

parameters.name: 'MaxAngularVelocity'
parameters.description: Saturation on the turn rate in rad/s.

tools.name: imufilter
tools.description: Fuse accelerometer and gyroscope measurements with a complementary Kalman filter to estimate orientation. It corrects gyroscope drift using gravity sensed by the accelerometer, but cannot observe heading about the gravity vector. Use it for tilt estimation when no magnetometer is available or trusted.
tools.usage:
FUSE = imufilter
FUSE = imufilter(Name, Value)
[orientation, angularVelocity] = FUSE(accelReadings, gyroReadings)
reset(FUSE)

parameters.name: 'DecimationFactor'
parameters.description: Output decimation relative to the input rate.

tools.notes: Heading (yaw) drifts without a magnetometer; use ahrsfilter when one is available.

tools.name: ahrsfilter
tools.description: Fuse accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer readings into a full 3-D orientation estimate including absolute heading. It models and rejects magnetic disturbances and estimates gyroscope bias online. Use it for attitude and heading reference on drones, wearables and handheld devices.
tools.usage:
FUSE = ahrsfilter
FUSE = ahrsfilter(Name, Value)
[orientation, angularVelocity] = FUSE(accelReadings, gyroReadings, magReadings)
reset(FUSE); tune(FUSE, sensorData, groundTruth)

tools.name: insfilterMARG
tools.description: An extended Kalman filter that fuses MARG (magnetic, angular rate and gravity) sensor data with GPS position and velocity to estimate pose, velocity and sensor biases. It exposes separate predict and fuse methods so asynchronous sensors can be incorporated at their own rates. Use it for full inertial navigation on a UAV or vehicle.
tools.usage:
filt = insfilterMARG
filt = insfilterMARG(Name, Value)
predict(filt, accelData, gyroData)
fusegps(filt, position, Rpos, velocity, Rvel)
fusemag(filt, magData, Rmag)
[position, orientation, velocity] = pose(filt)

parameters.name: 'ReferenceLocation'
parameters.description: [lat lon alt] origin of the local navigation frame.

parameters.name: 'GeomagneticVectorNoise'
parameters.description: Uncertainty in the reference magnetic field.

tools.notes: insfilterAsync, insfilterErrorState and insfilterNonholonomic are variants for different sensor sets and vehicle constraints.

tools.name: lidarScan
tools.description: Represent a 2-D lidar scan as ranges and angles with the corresponding Cartesian points computed automatically. It provides methods to remove invalid readings, transform the scan into another frame and plot it. It is the input type for scan matching, SLAM and occupancy map updates.
tools.usage:
scan = lidarScan(ranges, angles)
scan = lidarScan(cartesianPoints)
validScan = removeInvalidData(scan, Name, Value)
transformedScan = transformScan(scan, relPose)
plot(scan)

parameters.name: ranges
parameters.description: Vector of range measurements in metres.

parameters.name: relPose
parameters.description: [x y theta] relative pose used by transformScan.
